chapters.narration: Welcome to your agent teamwork upgrade! No artificial intelligence doctorate required. Imagine a tiny support team: one person keeps the goal straight, another investigates, another builds, and another reviews. We will give Copilot similarly clear jobs, rather than asking a crowd of helpers to change everything at once. Our practice app is an issue triage board with fictional support tickets. It is deliberately small. We will add priority, search, a summary, and an evidence export. The interesting part is how we direct the work, protect shared files, and check that the final result actually works. This is a visual lesson with an artificial intelligence generated voice, not a recording of live product clicks. Pause whenever you want to try an example. The live workshop still lasts three hours: one hour of presentation and demonstrations, followed by two hours of hands-on labs.

chapters.title: What you will be able to do
items: Choose instructions, a custom agent, or a skill for the right job
Delegate a bounded task with an evidence-based result
Coordinate one repository without overlapping writers
Review and integrate changes instead of trusting completion messages
chapters.narration: Here is the whole workshop in three pieces. A custom agent is a reusable job description. A skill is a reusable recipe with supporting files. Your prompt is today's task: what to change, what to leave alone, and how to prove success. Different jobs need different tools, not bigger promises. You will learn to give a helper a small, complete assignment. It needs the goal, the relevant context, the files it may edit, and the result to return. That result should contain evidence and unresolved questions. A confident sentence saying finished is not the same as a verified change. You will also learn why two chats can collide in one repository. Separate conversations do not guarantee separate files. We will compare clear ownership, a single integration writer, dependency ordering, and separate worktrees. The best choice is the simplest workflow that keeps the changes understandable and safe.

chapters.title: Five words that prevent confusion
items: Model: generates and reasons about possible next actions
Harness: manages context, tool calls, approvals and execution
Custom agent: reusable role + instructions + selected tools
Subagent: delegated work in a separate context
Skill: an on-demand procedure with supporting resources
chapters.narration: A model proposes the next useful action. The harness is the control room around it: it supplies context, tools, permissions, and execution. A tool is an action such as reading a file or running a test. Changing the model does not automatically change the harness or its configuration format. A custom agent is a definition of a specialist. A subagent is a helper doing delegated work in a separate context. You can select a specialist yourself, or a main agent can call it for a side task. Built-in helpers can be subagents too; you do not need a new profile for every task. Context means the notes available to the helper. A session is an ongoing unit of work with its conversation and workspace. Two notebooks can sit on the same desk. Likewise, two separate contexts can still edit the same checkout. Keep the job definition, the delegated call, and the actual workspace separate in your thinking.

chapters.title: Separate context is not separate files
items: Two chats can point at the same checkout
Subagents do not automatically receive independent worktrees
A worktree separates working files, not machine permissions
An approval mode is not a filesystem lock
chapters.narration: Here is our first collision. Two helpers have separate conversations, but both reach for the same file. One edit can overwrite the other. Subagents do not automatically get independent worktrees. A separate chat is useful for focus, but it is not evidence of filesystem isolation. Three protections answer three different questions. A worktree separates working copies. Tool permissions control actions that need approval. A sandbox can restrict access to files, networks, or credentials. None is a substitute for the others. A worktree is another workbench, not a locked room around your computer. Collisions are not limited to source code. Helpers in one checkout share its branch and Git index. Servers can fight over a port, and tests can overwrite a report directory. Before parallel writing, identify all the writable surfaces. If the boundaries are unclear, serialize the writes.

items: Projects coordinate an ongoing goal; sessions perform scoped work

chapters.narration: The GitHub Copilot app is a desktop home for agent-driven development on Windows, macOS, and Linux. A Project can coordinate an ongoing goal; a session performs a bounded task. For this workshop, one repository and one small feature are enough. The diagram is an orientation sketch, not a screenshot of your build. When starting a session, choose the environment and workspace deliberately. New worktree gives a separate working copy. Current checkout uses the existing files and can overlap another writer. Read the selector and confirm the actual path. Do not assume the app's parallel sessions make every task independent. Plan lets you review an approach first. Interactive supports collaborative steering. Autopilot suits a clear task. Tool permissions are a separate choice: they decide which actions need approval. More autonomy does not remove your responsibility to inspect the changes and verify the outcome before integration.

chapters.title: Direct one small task, then inspect it
items: Select the starter repository and verify workspace
Use Plan: outcome + constraints + acceptance checks
Approve a bounded change with appropriate permissions

chapters.narration: For the app demonstration, ask for a plan to add one triage behavior. Include the expected result, allowed files, and existing test commands. Ask it not to edit yet. The useful output is a bounded plan with affected paths and checks, not a proposal to rebuild the application. Review the plan. Reject surprise dependencies, databases, or unrelated improvements. Then allow the bounded implementation. Watch the changed files while it works. If it drifts, correct the same session with a concrete instruction. Confirm the active workspace before giving feedback; another conversation may be working on a different task. When it finishes, read the complete relevant diff and run the checks. Try the actual behavior in the board. An agent's completion message is not the acceptance criterion. If the desktop app is unavailable, do the same plan, implement, and review loop in VS Code.

chapters.title: An agent-first window beside your editor
items: Command Palette: Chat: Open Agents window

Sessions + Customizations | conversation | Files + Changes

chapters.narration: VS Code's Agents window puts agent work first, beside the normal editor. Open it with the command Chat: Open Agents window, or code, double dash agents. The sidebar organizes sessions and customizations, the center holds the conversation, and the review pane shows files and changes. Actual controls may vary with your build. Several panes can be visible, but only one is active. Select the intended session before feedback, terminal commands, or browser checks. Branch mode uses the selected current folder. New Worktree starts from committed files in a separate directory. Separate panes alone do not isolate edits. Supported sessions can continue between the editor and Agents window without starting over. Cloud and remote sessions have additional requirements; a remote host must remain available. We keep the core labs local, so you can see the paths, run the commands, and understand exactly where the changes go.

chapters.title: Select the harness before copying YAML
items: Copilot: native task delegation; skills field supported
Local: agent/runSubagent; agents allowlist + handoffs

target selects file interpretation, not the running harness
chapters.narration: Sharing an agent filename does not guarantee identical behavior across harnesses. Copilot uses native task delegation and supports a skills field. Local uses the run subagent tool and supports a named agents allowlist and handoffs. These are different contracts. Check both the schema and actual available tools. The target field tells the editor how to interpret the file. Target vscode means Local interpretation; target github-copilot means Copilot interpretation. It does not switch your session's harness. Select the harness in the interface first. A completion suggestion is helpful, but it does not prove the runtime supports that tool. Do not paste Local's agents list or handoffs into a Copilot example and expect enforcement. Do not paste Copilot's skills field into Local. The repository has separate examples. If native delegation is missing, run the same roles sequentially with a written handoff. The learning goal is reliable work, not a particular button.

chapters.title: Write a task contract, not a wish
items: Goal and concrete acceptance examples
Relevant files, constraints and non-goals
Allowed actions and explicit write ownership
Tests + evidence + a stopping condition
chapters.narration: Make this smarter is a wish. Add this exact priority rule, preserve the issue shape, edit only this module and its tests, and run these checks is a task contract. The agent still chooses implementation details, but it no longer needs to invent your business requirements. Provide acceptance examples. One case should trigger the new behavior, one should remain unchanged, and one should test the exact boundary. Give the relevant files and existing commands. These examples are more useful than a long persona description or an instruction to be brilliant. Finish the brief with the expected report and a stopping condition. Return changed paths, exact checks, results, and remaining risks. Stop when the assigned behavior passes, or report a specific blocker. Do not expand into unrelated cleanup. Small, self-contained briefs make delegation easier to evaluate.
chapters.code:
GOAL: implement one named behavior
CONTEXT: contract + relevant files + examples
WRITE SET: module A + tests A only
CHECKS: exact commands and expected results
RETURN: evidence, risks, blocked decisions
STOP: no unrelated improvements

chapters.title: A reviewer that can read, not write
items: A focused role beats a grandiose persona
Use only tools the role needs
Define useful findings and honest uncertainty
chapters.narration: Our first specialist is a reviewer. Its job is to find incorrect behavior and missing tests in the assigned files, then return actionable findings. It does not need to implement the fix. A focused role is easier to verify than a grand persona such as ultimate expert in everything. Give this reviewer reading and search tools, not editing or terminal execution. Define the report: file, problem, impact, and suggested fix or test. Check actual runtime activity because restrictions differ by harness. A read-only reviewer must not claim it ran tests; execution evidence comes from someone with execution tools. Start a fresh session with the intended harness and a small file you understand. Ask for a review without repeating the role instructions. Inspect the findings against the source and look at tool activity and workspace changes. Listed in the picker is discovery, not proof that the agent behaves correctly.
chapters.code:
---
name: Workshop Reviewer
description: Review behavior and missing tests
tools: ['read', 'search']
---
Read the assigned source and tests.
Do not edit or run commands.
Return file, issue, impact and suggested test.
State what you could not verify.

chapters.title: A reusable recipe with a trigger
items: Folder: .github/skills/test-changes/
Required: SKILL.md name + description
Name matches folder; describe WHAT and WHEN
Resources and scripts stay with the skill
chapters.narration: A skill is a folder containing a procedure and any supporting resources. Our triage-policy skill has a SKILL dot markdown file, a policy reference, and a fixture inspection script. Copy the whole folder, not just the headline file. Otherwise the recipe can point at missing ingredients. The skill needs a name and description in frontmatter. The lowercase, hyphenated name must match the directory. The description explains what it does and when to use it. Refer to supporting files with paths relative to SKILL dot markdown. Keep the steps concrete and tied to the repository. Verify explicit invocation, then test a matching ordinary request separately. Automatic selection is useful, not guaranteed. Check whether the agent read the resource and used the right command. A skill does not grant tools or credentials. A reader-only role can describe a check, but cannot truthfully execute it.
chapters.code:
---
name: test-changes
description: Validate code changes with the
  repository tests; use before a handoff.
---
1. Read the repository test commands.
2. Run checks for the assigned change.
3. Report passed / failed / not run.
Use [report format](./references/report.md).

chapters.title: Discovery is not execution evidence
items: Metadata first; full procedure when relevant
References and scripts loaded only as needed
Test positive, negative and ambiguous requests
No automatic grants of credentials or tools
chapters.narration: These are four different checkpoints. A skill can exist on disk without discovery. It can be discovered without selection. It can be selected without successfully running its script. Do not collapse the whole chain into a green installed badge. Inspect the actual activity and the result. Test a request that clearly matches the skill, one that should not use it, and one that is ambiguous. For triage policy, changing priority should load the policy. Explaining the page layout should not need to run priority checks. Refine the description when observed behavior is wrong. Review scripts and resources before using an acquired skill. A skill supplies a recipe; an MCP connection exposes external tools. Approve and review those tools separately. Marketplace availability is not a trust guarantee. The report should distinguish passed, failed, and not run. Missing capability must not become a success-shaped answer.

chapters.title: Compose them without mixing harnesses
items: Copilot agent: skills: ['test-changes']
Local agent: ask it to load the relevant skill
Both: narrow tools and explicit success criteria
Verify the enabled skill inventory in a fresh session
chapters.narration: Now combine the parts. The implementer is responsible for one change. The triage policy supplies a repeated procedure. The task brief supplies today's acceptance examples and allowed files. This is composition, not magic: each part has a clear responsibility that you can inspect. Copilot supports naming enabled skills in the agent's skills field. Use the exact skill name and confirm the inventory and actual loading. Preloading is not execution proof. The worker still needs appropriate tools and approvals, and the task still needs a narrow write set. Local does not accept that Copilot skills field. Use its supported discovery or explicit invocation instead. Do not give a researcher terminal access merely because an implementer uses a test procedure. Compose only what the role needs, then verify the behavior in the selected harness.
chapters.code:
# Copilot harness example
---
name: Bounded Implementer
description: Implement one assigned change
target: github-copilot
tools: ['read', 'search', 'edit', 'execute']
skills: ['test-changes']
---
Stay in the assigned write set.

items: Research the issue input and rule boundary

chapters.narration: Let's make the priority example concrete. Active issues start at sixty points for high impact, thirty for medium, or ten for low. A blocked workflow adds twenty-five. At least one hundred affected users adds ten. At least seven days old adds five. Our first issue totals one hundred points. P one starts at eighty points, P two at forty, and lower scores are P three. This additive policy cannot produce exactly eighty, so test the nearest reachable scores: seventy-five is P two, eighty-five is P one. Also test ninety-nine versus one hundred users and six versus seven days. Closed issues override the bonuses: zero points, P three, and only the closed-issue reason. Research the contract, implement one owned module, run those cases, then request review. This demo proves a requirement, not merely that an agent wrote code. Lab two supplies the complete specification.

chapters.narration: Before parallel writing, spot the hot files: shared contracts, package manifests, lockfiles, server wiring, and common fixtures. Different branches in the same folder do not give separate workspaces. Our offline sample removes databases and credentials so the remaining boundaries are easy to see. If a worker needs another path, request a new assignment. Markdown and chat claims are protocols, not operating-system mutexes. Actual locking requires an enforcement mechanism with defined failure behavior. Do not market a task board as a built-in cross-agent security boundary.

chapters.title: Review, hand off and reflect
items: Inspect all changed files and requirement coverage
Run the final quality gates and user-flow check
Write evidence, risks and remaining decisions
Explain where parallelism helped or hurt
chapters.narration: You have fifteen minutes. Review the complete relevant diff and requirement coverage. Run the final checks and user flow, then create the minimal evidence export. Mark unavailable checks not run with a reason. Do not turn missing evidence into a success statement. Write a handoff someone can use without reading the whole agent history. Include the outcome, changed paths, assumptions, exact checks and results, remaining risks, and next decisions. An evidence-based handoff is the final product, not an agent completion message. Ask which tasks were truly independent, whether separate contexts helped, and where coordination cost more than a direct edit. The live workshop ends at three hours. Hooks, marketplace packaging, and cloud continuity are optional extensions afterward, not hidden extra requirements.

chapters.title: Reliable orchestration is an engineering skill
items: Role + recipe + task contract
Separate context != isolated workspace
Independent tasks + explicit ownership + one integrator
Evidence beats confident prose
chapters.narration: Your reliable teamwork recipe is a role, a reusable procedure, and a specific task contract. Choose narrow responsibilities and real acceptance examples. The agent owns a job, the skill supplies a process, and the prompt defines what success means today. Separate context does not mean separate files. Freeze contracts, assign owners, serialize shared changes, and use one integrator. Worktrees help separate working copies; permissions and sandboxing solve different problems. Advisory claims help coordination but do not enforce a lock. Evidence beats confident prose. A read-only reviewer cannot claim it ran tests. Target vscode does not switch the harness. Two passing branches can fail together, so retest after integration. Keep the smallest workflow that reliably proves the outcome. That's the upgrade from agent user to orchestrator.
